passage:
Rafael stood by the coat hooks, watching. A boy in a dinosaur jumper lined up toy cars. Two girls whispered over a puzzle. Which one would be his friend? He kept his hands in his pockets and leaned towards the cars, then back again.
Javier, the teacher, clapped softly. "Pairs, please! Each pair builds one tall tower." He set Rafael beside the dinosaur boy, Tomas, and handed them a box of paper cups.
Tomas held up a cup. "Yours goes on top."
Rafael almost smiled and put it there.

qa.q: What did Tomas have on his jumper?
qa.a: He wore a dinosaur jumper.

qa.q: How does Rafael feel as he watches the other children?
qa.a: He feels shy and curious: he keeps his hands in his pockets and leans towards the cars, then back, wondering who will be his friend.

qa.q: How did Javier help friendships begin?
qa.a: He paired children for a shared job, building a tower, so Rafael and Tomas had something to do together instead of having to start a conversation. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tomas see the new boy beside him?
qa.a: He seems friendly and welcoming, since he hands Rafael a cup and lets him put it on top.

grounding: A new child watches the others and wonders who will be his friend, feeling shy and curious; the teacher pairs children for an activity.

passage:
Rain kept everyone inside, and the canteen was so loud that Avni had to lean in to hear Kashish. Only it was Kashish who was leaning towards Meera, the new girl, and laughing at something Avni had not heard. Avni's stomach twisted.
The words came fast in her head: Meera copies everything. Nobody likes her. She pressed her lips together and pushed her rice around.
When the bell rang, she caught Kashish's sleeve. "I miss sitting with you. Just us, I mean."
Kashish blinked, then softened. "I miss it too. Saturday? Your house?"
Avni nodded, her chest lighter.

qa.q: Where were the girls sitting when Avni felt her stomach twist?
qa.a: They were in the noisy canteen because rain kept everyone inside.

qa.q: Why did Avni press her lips together instead of saying what she was thinking about Meera?
qa.a: She was jealous, but she chose not to run Meera down, because sulking or spreading talk would only push Kashish away.

qa.q: What worked for Avni and why?
qa.a: She said plainly that she missed Kashish and asked for time just the two of them, which asked for closeness without blaming anyone. 🙂

qa.q: How might Kashish have seen the moment?
qa.a: She may have been unaware Avni was hurting, and she is relieved and warm when Avni says it kindly.

grounding: A girl feels jealous when her best friend laughs with the new girl, and says she misses her instead of sulking or stealing her back.

passage:
Tuesday night, very tired.
All week I have been checking where Hafsa sits: the bus, the lunch bench, the art table. Today she sat with Tanvi again. I asked her why three times. Her face went tight and she said, "Nitin, you are everywhere." My ears burned.
Then I finally said the true thing: "I feel left out. Can we do one thing just us?"
She was quiet, then said, "Saturday, cycling?"
I am still a little scared she will like Tanvi more. But my stomach does not hurt as much now. 🙂
- Nitin

qa.q: Where did Hafsa suggest going with Nitin on Saturday?
qa.a: She suggested cycling.

qa.q: What was Nitin afraid of all week?
qa.a: He was afraid of being replaced by Tanvi, so he kept checking where Hafsa sat.

qa.q: What worked better than checking where she sits?
qa.a: Telling her plainly that he felt left out and asking for one plan just for them worked better, since checking made her feel trapped.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt when Nitin asked three times?
qa.a: She felt crowded and a bit trapped, which she said with a tight face and by saying he was everywhere.

grounding: A boy fears being replaced, checks who his friend sits with, then says he feels left out and asks for one plan just for the two of them.

passage:
I am Mridul, and that autumn Aarav from the chess club started sitting with me and became a friend. Suddenly Sumit, my best friend since Class 1, stopped saving my seat on the bus. He answered in one word and looked out of the window.
I felt guilty, as if I had done something wrong, and cornered too, because I did not want to give up either of them.
So I told him, "You are still my best friend." We kept our Saturday cricket, just us. And one afternoon I asked if he wanted to play chess with Aarav and me. He shrugged, but he came.

qa.q: Where did Mridul meet Aarav?
qa.a: He met Aarav in the chess club.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when Sumit turned cold?
qa.a: He felt guilty and cornered, as if he had done something wrong but could not give up either friend.

qa.q: Why was it not necessary for Mridul to drop Aarav?
qa.a: Sumit needed reassurance and time together, not a lost friend, so Mridul kept their Saturday cricket and invited him in.

qa.q: How might Sumit have seen the chess club friendship?
qa.a: He seems to fear being replaced, since he stops saving the seat and answers in one word, but he still comes when invited.

grounding: A boy's best friend goes cold after he makes a new friend; he feels guilty and cornered, reassures him, keeps their special time and invites him in.

passage:
Monday: At lunch Amandeep played tag with Jatin, the new boy, and it was the best game all term. Then she saw Ishita watching from the doorway, holding her lunchbox, and her stomach dropped, as if she had done something bad.
Wednesday: "Where were you Saturday?" Ishita asked. "At my cousin's," said Amandeep. It was untrue. She had been at Jatin's. The lie sat in her chest all afternoon.
Friday: She found Ishita by the swings. "I was at Jatin's. I like him. But you still matter to me. Do you want to play with us?"

qa.q: Who was watching from the doorway on Monday?
qa.a: Ishita was watching, holding her lunchbox.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep's stomach drop when she saw Ishita?
qa.a: She liked playing with Jatin but felt like a traitor to her old friend, as if she had done something bad.

qa.q: What made things worse, and what made them better?
qa.a: The lie on Wednesday made it worse and weighed on her; telling the truth, saying Ishita still matters and inviting her made it better.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt hearing where Amandeep had been?
qa.a: She was probably hurt at first, but she may also have felt respected that Amandeep told the truth and included her.

grounding: A girl likes a new friend but feels like a traitor to her old friend; a lie makes it worse until she tells the truth and includes the old friend.

passage:
Sarita, even Vijay Uncle was small once. When I was your age, we moved to Nashik and I started Class 5 in a new school. On the first week a boy called Ramesh shared his tiffin with me and we became friends. His old friend Sunil, though, never smiled at me. He turned away when I came near. I felt it in my stomach.
I did not say a word against Sunil to Ramesh. I said good morning to both of them every day, and never asked Ramesh to pick a side.
Months later, Sunil passed me a cricket bat. Nothing more. But it was enough.
Give it time, Sarita.

qa.q: Where did Vijay move when he was young?
qa.a: He moved to Nashik and started Class 5 in a new school.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel about Sunil turning away?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and unwelcome, sensing Sunil disliked him, which he felt in his stomach.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that worked?
qa.a: He stayed friendly to both boys, did not badmouth Sunil, did not ask Ramesh to choose, and gave it time.

qa.q: How might Sunil have seen Vijay at the start?
qa.a: He may have felt threatened by the newcomer taking his friend's attention, which could explain the turning away.

grounding: A newcomer senses his new friend's old friend dislikes him, stays friendly, does not force a choice and gives it time.

passage:
I'm Irawati and I sit behind Sarika in Class 4. On Thursday I watched her best friend Nisha talking with the new girl, Pooja, by the water tank. Sarika stopped a few steps away and rubbed her sleeve. I can't say what she felt, but she stayed there for a moment.
Then she walked up. "Hi, Pooja. I'm Sarika." And to Nisha, quietly, "I like sitting with you, but a game is more fun with three. Want to play catch?"
Nisha grinned. Pooja nodded. They spent the whole break tossing the ball, all three laughing.

qa.q: Where did Nisha talk with Pooja?
qa.a: They talked by the water tank.

qa.q: What might Sarika have been feeling when she stopped and rubbed her sleeve?
qa.a: She may have felt a small pang or unsure, though Irawati says she cannot tell exactly what Sarika felt.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that turned it into a game for three?
qa.a: She said hi to Pooja, told Nisha honestly what she liked, and suggested catch for three.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when Sarika came over?
qa.a: She was probably glad to be included, since she nodded and joined the game.

grounding: A girl sees that her friend can have other friends, says hi to the new girl and suggests a game for three, without pretending to feel nothing.

passage:
Thursday.
Today Yash sat with Dev again at lunch, and they laughed at a joke I did not hear. I ate fast and read my book. My cousin said "just ignore it" on the phone. That made me feel worse, like there was nothing to say.
In the evening Mum came and sat on my bed. "You have been quiet, Lokesh. Want to tell me?"
So I did. She said friendships shift and stretch, that this doesn't mean it is over, and that she would always be close by. I cried a little. 🙂
I still feel sad, but I do not feel so alone.
Lokesh

qa.q: Who did Yash sit with at lunch?
qa.a: He sat with Dev.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh feel worse after his cousin said "just ignore it"?
qa.a: It made him feel alone with the hurt, as if there was nothing to say.

qa.q: What did Mum do that helped Lokesh?
qa.a: She noticed he was quiet, sat on his bed, listened, and said friendships shift and stretch and that she would be close by.

qa.q: How might Lokesh's cousin have meant the advice?
qa.a: The cousin probably meant to help him not to fret, though it did not make him feel heard.

grounding: A boy is quiet after his friend gets a new friend; his mum listens and says friendships shift and stretch, so he feels heard.

passage:
Kite season had come to the village, and Kunal held the spool tight while Meenu flew the red kite. Then two girls called her to the roof steps. She handed over the string and ran.
"You are my friend, not theirs!" Kunal shouted, grabbing her wrist. Meenu's face closed. She pulled free and walked away.
Samir Uncle looked up from his tea stall. "Why the long face?"
Kunal muttered it out. Samir pointed at the kite. "It flies high because the string lets out. Pull it too tight and it drops."
Next day Kunal said, "Go and play," and Meenu came back at lunch.

qa.q: What colour was the kite Meenu flew?
qa.a: It was a red kite.

qa.q: Why did Kunal shout at Meenu when she went off with the two girls?
qa.a: He was angry, and it felt like caring to him, but he was treating her as if she belonged only to him.

qa.q: What did Samir Uncle's kite example teach Kunal?
qa.a: That holding a friend too tightly makes her pull away, and that letting her go trusts she will come back.

qa.q: How might Meenu have felt when Kunal grabbed her wrist?
qa.a: She likely felt shrunk and cornered, since her face closed and she pulled away and walked off.

grounding: A boy treats his friend like property and gets angry when she plays with others; an uncle shows him a kite string that needs slack.

passage:
Deepak said, "Fine, go play with Tara," and watched Mahima run to the colony park, where the new girl waited. He kicked a pebble. That was the third time this week she had picked someone else. He counted them like coins: Monday at lunch, Tuesday on the swings, now this.
He kept the list in his head all evening and felt hot every time he looked at it. A mean sentence about Tara rose to his tongue.
Instead, the next morning he said, quietly, "It hurt when you chose Tara at lunch. I just wanted you to know."
Mahima looked surprised. "Oh. I didn't think."

qa.q: How many times had Mahima picked someone else this week, by Deepak's count?
qa.a: Three times, counting Monday at lunch, Tuesday on the swings, and now.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling as he kept a list in his head?
qa.a: He was hurt and resentful, feeling hot each time he looked at it, even though he had said fine.

qa.q: What could Deepak do that worked better than counting silently?
qa.a: He could say calmly, once, that it hurt, as he did the next morning, rather than let the list grow.

qa.q: How might Mahima have seen it before Deepak spoke?
qa.a: She probably had no idea, since she says she did not think, and only saw a friend saying fine.

grounding: A boy says 'fine' but silently counts every time his friend chose others, then says the hurt out loud once, calmly.
